It is the cornerstone of therapy for adrenal carcinoma but has a slow onset of action and significant gastrointestinal and neurological toxicity.

medical_therapies.mechanism: This drug blocks the action of cortisol at the peripheral glucocorticoid receptor, mitigating its effects without lowering cortisol levels.
medical_therapies.agents: * **Mifepristone (RU-486)**: A potent antagonist at the glucocorticoid receptor. It is used to control hyperglycemia in patients with Cushing syndrome who are not surgical candidates or have failed other treatments. Note: Cortisol levels will rise due to loss of negative feedback, so they cannot be used to monitor therapy.

management: Post-Surgical Care: Monitor for remission with 24-hour UFC or late-night salivary cortisol. Patients often require temporary (after unilateral adrenalectomy or TSS) or permanent (after bilateral adrenalectomy) glucocorticoid replacement therapy due to HPA axis suppression.
Lifelong Replacement (post-bilateral adrenalectomy): Requires both glucocorticoid (hydrocortisone) and mineralocorticoid (fludrocortisone) replacement, with patient education on stress dosing.
Comorbidity Management: Aggressive and ongoing treatment of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, and osteoporosis.
Long-Term Surveillance: Regular clinical follow-up and biochemical testing to monitor for disease recurrence. Periodic imaging (e.g., pituitary MRI) may be indicated based on etiology.
Psychiatric Support: Address persistent mood, anxiety, and cognitive symptoms, which may not fully resolve after biochemical cure.

diagnostics.overview: The diagnostic approach to Cushing syndrome is a systematic, multi-step process designed to first confirm the presence of pathological hypercortisolism, and then to accurately pinpoint its underlying etiology. The initial step involves screening with highly sensitive tests to overcome the diagnostic challenge of overlapping symptoms with common conditions like metabolic syndrome. Because cortisol secretion is pulsatile and follows a diurnal rhythm, single random measurements are unreliable. Therefore, screening relies on integrated measures (24-hour urinary free cortisol), assessing the nadir of secretion (late-night salivary cortisol), or testing the integrity of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis negative feedback (low-dose dexamethasone suppression test). Once hypercortisolism is confirmed, the second critical step is to measure plasma ACTH to differentiate between ACTH-dependent causes (pituitary or ectopic tumors) and ACTH-independent causes (adrenal pathology). This bifurcation dictates the subsequent diagnostic pathway. The final step involves localization studies, combining dynamic endocrine testing (e.g., high-dose dexamethasone suppression, CRH stimulation) and high-resolution imaging (e.g., pituitary MRI, adrenal CT) to identify the precise location of the tumor, which is essential for guiding definitive therapy.

diagnostic_steps.title: Confirming Hypercortisolism (Screening)
diagnostic_steps.description: Initial testing to establish the presence of cortisol excess. At least two different first-line tests should be abnormal to confirm the diagnosis.

tests.name: 24-Hour Urinary Free Cortisol (UFC)
tests.mechanism: Measures the total amount of unbound, biologically active cortisol excreted by the kidneys over a full day. This integrates cortisol production over 24 hours, bypassing the issue of pulsatile secretion and providing a robust indicator of total daily cortisol output. Values >3-4 times the upper limit of normal are highly suggestive of Cushing syndrome.
tests.pearl: Requires a complete and accurately timed 24-hour urine collection. Creatinine measurement is used to verify collection adequacy.

tests.name: Late-Night Salivary Cortisol
tests.mechanism: Capitalizes on the loss of the normal diurnal rhythm of cortisol. In healthy individuals, cortisol levels reach a nadir between 11 PM and midnight. In Cushing syndrome, this nadir is lost, resulting in elevated late-night levels. Saliva reflects the free, active fraction of cortisol.
tests.pearl: Convenient for outpatient testing. Samples should be collected on at least two separate nights. Avoid vigorous brushing or eating immediately before collection.

tests.name: 1-mg Overnight Dexamethasone Suppression Test (LDDST)
tests.mechanism: This tests the integrity of the HPA axis's negative feedback loop. A synthetic glucocorticoid, dexamethasone (1 mg), is given at 11 PM. In a normal individual, this exogenous steroid suppresses the pituitary's release of ACTH, leading to low serum cortisol (<1.8 mcg/dL) the following morning. In Cushing syndrome, the autonomous source of cortisol (or ACTH) is not suppressed by this low dose.
tests.pearl: False positives can occur due to factors that increase dexamethasone metabolism (e.g., anticonvulsants) or in conditions of 'pseudo-Cushing's' like depression or alcoholism.

diagnostic_steps.title: Determining ACTH-Dependency
diagnostic_steps.description: Once hypercortisolism is confirmed, the next step is to measure a baseline plasma ACTH level to classify the etiology.

interpretation.explanation: An adrenal tumor (adenoma or carcinoma) is autonomously producing cortisol. This high level of cortisol exerts negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary, suppressing CRH and ACTH production. The next step is adrenal imaging (CT/MRI).

Excess ACTH from either a pituitary adenoma (Cushing's Disease) or an ectopic source (e.g., small cell lung cancer) is overstimulating the adrenal glands to produce cortisol. The next step is to differentiate between a pituitary and an ectopic source.

diagnostic_steps.title: Localizing the Source of ACTH Excess
diagnostic_steps.description: For ACTH-dependent cases, further testing is required to differentiate a pituitary source (Cushing's disease, ~80% of cases) from an ectopic source.

tests.name: High-Dose Dexamethasone Suppression Test (HDDST)
tests.mechanism: Pituitary adenomas in Cushing's disease, while autonomous, often retain partial sensitivity to strong negative feedback. An 8-mg dose of dexamethasone is typically sufficient to suppress ACTH secretion from the adenoma, leading to a >50% reduction in cortisol levels. Ectopic ACTH-producing tumors are generally completely resistant to feedback and will not suppress.
tests.pearl: This test has been largely superseded by IPSS due to imperfect sensitivity and specificity but is still a key board exam concept.

tests.name: CRH Stimulation Test
tests.mechanism: Pituitary corticotroph adenomas typically express CRH receptors and will respond to exogenous CRH with an exaggerated increase in ACTH and cortisol. Ectopic tumors usually lack these receptors and show no response.
tests.pearl: Can be combined with inferior petrosal sinus sampling for greater accuracy.

tests.name: Inferior Petrosal Sinus Sampling (IPSS)
tests.mechanism: This is the gold standard for differentiating pituitary from ectopic sources. Catheters are placed in the inferior petrosal sinuses, which directly drain the pituitary gland. ACTH levels are measured simultaneously from the sinuses and a peripheral vein, both at baseline and after CRH stimulation. A high central-to-peripheral ACTH gradient (typically >2:1 at baseline or >3:1 post-CRH) confirms a pituitary source.
tests.pearl: An invasive procedure with risks, reserved for cases where non-invasive tests and imaging are equivocal.

diagnostic_steps.title: Imaging for Tumor Localization
diagnostic_steps.description: Imaging is performed only after biochemical tests have established the etiology, as incidentalomas are common.

studies.indication: Suspected Cushing's Disease (ACTH-dependent, positive IPSS or suppressible on HDDST). To identify the pituitary microadenoma (<1 cm) or macroadenoma (>1 cm).
studies.pearl: Up to 40% of microadenomas may not be visible on MRI, hence the reliance on biochemical testing like IPSS for confirmation.

studies.indication: Suspected adrenal cause (ACTH-independent). To identify a unilateral adrenal adenoma or carcinoma.
studies.pearl: CT can often differentiate benign adenomas (small, low-density) from suspicious malignant lesions (large, irregular, high-density).

studies.indication: Suspected ectopic ACTH syndrome. A comprehensive search for the primary tumor, most commonly found in the lungs (carcinoid, small cell lung cancer), pancreas, or thymus.
studies.pearl: If conventional imaging is negative, somatostatin receptor scintigraphy (Octreoscan) or PET scan may be used to locate the neuroendocrine tumor.

riskFactors: Most common: Long-term, high-dose exogenous glucocorticoid therapy.
Female sex (Cushing's Disease is 3-5 times more common in women).
Age 20-50 years.
Presence of adrenal or pituitary tumors.
Ectopic ACTH-producing tumors (e.g., small cell lung cancer, carcinoid tumors).
Rare genetic syndromes (e.g., Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1 [MEN1], Carney complex).
content.epidemiology: *   **Overall:** The most common cause is iatrogenic steroid use. *   **Endogenous:** Rare, with an incidence of 2-5 cases per million people per year. *   **Cushing's Disease:** More common in women (3:1 ratio), typically diagnosed between ages 20-50. *   **Ectopic ACTH Syndrome:** More common in men, reflecting the epidemiology of SCLC. *   **Adrenal Tumors:** More common in women.
examFindings: General: Central (truncal) obesity with slender extremities.
Face: Moon facies (round, plethoric face), hirsutism, acne.
Body: Dorsocervical fat pad ('buffalo hump'), supraclavicular fat pads.
Skin: Thin, atrophic skin; wide (>1 cm), violaceous (purple) striae on abdomen, thighs, and axillae; ecchymoses (easy bruising); telangiectasias; hyperpigmentation (only in ACTH-dependent causes).
Musculoskeletal: Proximal muscle wasting and weakness.
Cardiovascular: Hypertension, peripheral edema.
Neurologic: Cognitive impairment, emotional lability.
Ophthalmologic: Cataracts, increased intraocular pressure.
**Buffalo hump**: Dorsocervical fat pad
**Purple striae**: Wide stretch marks on abdomen
complications: Cardiovascular: Hypertension, myocardial infarction, stroke, congestive heart failure, venous thromboembolism (VTE).
Metabolic: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus, dyslipidemia.
Musculoskeletal: Osteoporosis leading to pathologic fractures (especially vertebral compression fractures), avascular necrosis of the femoral head.
Immunologic: Increased susceptibility to infections, including opportunistic infections, due to immunosuppression.
Neuropsychiatric: Severe depression, psychosis, long-term cognitive impairment.
Endocrine: Adrenal crisis (if steroids are withdrawn abruptly or replacement is inadequate), hypopituitarism (post-pituitary surgery/radiation).
Surgical: Risks of surgery include hemorrhage, infection, and damage to surrounding structures. Transsphenoidal surgery carries a risk of diabetes insipidus and CSF leak.
content.clinicalPresentation: The presentation is often insidious, developing over months to years. Patients typically present with a combination of progressive central weight gain, skin changes, and new-onset or worsening hypertension and diabetes.
content.etiologyPathophysiology: The etiology is broadly divided into exogenous (iatrogenic) and endogenous causes.  **1. Exogenous (Iatrogenic) *   Most common cause overall** *   Prolonged administration of high-dose glucocorticoids (e.g., prednisone, dexamethasone) for inflammatory, autoimmune, or post-transplant conditions.  **2. Endogenous *   Rare** Endogenous causes are further classified by their dependence on ACTH.  *   **ACTH-Dependent (80% of endogenous cases)** *   **Cushing's Disease (70%):** A benign pituitary adenoma secretes excessive ACTH, leading to bilateral adrenal hyperplasia and hypercortisolism. *   **Ectopic ACTH Syndrome (10%):** A non-pituitary tumor (paraneoplastic) secretes ACTH. *   Most commonly **Small Cell Lung Cancer (SCLC)**. *   Other causes: Carcinoid tumors (bronchial, pancreatic), medullary thyroid cancer, pheochromocytoma.  *   **ACTH-Independent (20% of endogenous cases)** *   **Adrenal Adenoma (10%):** A benign cortisol-producing tumor on one adrenal gland. *   **Adrenal Carcinoma (5%):** A malignant cortisol-producing tumor. Often produces very high cortisol levels. *   **Micronodular or Macronodular Adrenal Hyperplasia (rare):** Both adrenal glands are enlarged and overproduce cortisol independent of ACTH.  **Pathophysiology:** Excess cortisol exerts exaggerated effects on multiple organ systems: *   **Metabolic:** Increases gluconeogenesis, lipolysis, and proteolysis, leading to hyperglycemia, central fat redistribution, and muscle wasting. *   **Catabolic:** Breaks down collagen in skin (thinning, striae) and bone (osteoporosis). *   **Immunosuppressive:** Inhibits immune function, increasing risk of infection. *   **Cardiovascular:** Increases vascular sensitivity to catecholamines and can have mineralocorticoid effects, leading to hypertension and hypokalemia. *   **CNS:** Affects mood, sleep, and cognition.

content.overview: Addison Disease is **primary adrenal insufficiency**, characterized by the destruction or dysfunction of the entire adrenal cortex. This results in a combined deficiency of **glucocorticoids (cortisol)**, **mineralocorticoids (aldosterone)**, and **adrenal androgens**. The lack of these critical hormones leads to a chronic, progressive, and potentially life-threatening condition marked by an inability to maintain blood pressure, blood glucose, and fluid/electrolyte balance, especially during periods of physiologic stress.
symptoms: Chronic, worsening fatigue and generalized weakness
Hyperpigmentation of skin and mucous membranes (bronze-like skin, darkening of palmar creases, buccal mucosa)
Anorexia and unintentional weight loss
Orthostatic hypotension (dizziness upon standing)
Salt craving
Gastrointestinal disturbances (nausea, vomiting, chronic abdominal pain, diarrhea)
Myalgias and arthralgias
In women: loss of libido, amenorrhea, decreased axillary and pubic hair
content.prognosis: With proper diagnosis, hormone replacement, and patient education on sick day management, the prognosis is excellent, and life expectancy is near-normal. Mortality is primarily associated with delayed diagnosis or mismanagement of an adrenal crisis.
treatment: **Chronic Maintenance Therapy:**

* **Glucocorticoid Replacement:** Hydrocortisone 15-25 mg/day orally, divided into 2-3 doses to mimic diurnal rhythm (e.g., 10-15 mg in AM, 5-10 mg in early PM). Prednisone can be used as an alternative.
* **Mineralocorticoid Replacement:** Fludrocortisone 0.05-0.2 mg orally once daily. Dosage is titrated to normalize blood pressure, orthostasis, sodium, and potassium levels.

* **Androgen Replacement:** DHEA 25-50 mg orally once daily may be considered for women with persistent fatigue, low mood, or decreased libido despite optimal glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid therapy.
**Acute Adrenal Crisis (Medical Emergency):**
* **Fluid Resuscitation:** Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation with 2-3 liters of Isotonic Saline (0.9% NaCl) or D5NS within the first 24 hours.
* **High-Dose Glucocorticoids:** Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus, followed by 200 mg/24 hours as a continuous infusion or 50 mg IV every 6 hours.
* **Supportive Care:** Correction of hypoglycemia, electrolyte abnormalities, and treatment of any precipitating cause (e.g., infection).
management: **Patient Education (Crucial):**

* **Sick Day Rules:** Patients must be instructed to double or triple their daily oral hydrocortisone dose during febrile illness, infection, or other physiologic stressors. Parenteral administration is required if unable to tolerate oral medication due to vomiting.
* **Emergency Preparedness:** Patients must wear a medical alert bracelet/necklace and carry an emergency card detailing their diagnosis and treatment.
* **Emergency Kit:** Every patient should possess an injectable hydrocortisone kit (e.g., 100 mg Solu-Cortef) and be trained, along with family members, on its administration for emergencies.
**Monitoring:**
* **Clinical Evaluation:** Regularly assess for signs of under-replacement (fatigue, weight loss, hyperpigmentation) or over-replacement (weight gain, edema, central obesity, hypertension).

* **Biochemical Monitoring:** Monitor serum sodium and potassium, and plasma renin activity to guide fludrocortisone dosing. The goal for renin is the high-normal range. Cortisol levels are not useful for monitoring therapy.
* **Bone Density:** Periodically monitor with DEXA scans to screen for steroid-induced osteoporosis.

diagnostics.overview: The diagnosis of Addison disease hinges on demonstrating an inappropriately low cortisol output from the adrenal cortex, coupled with evidence that the adrenal gland itself is the source of the failure. The diagnostic process is initiated based on a high index of suspicion from clinical signs (e.g., hyperpigmentation, orthostatic hypotension, salt craving) and non-specific symptoms (fatigue, weakness, weight loss). Initial laboratory tests often reveal characteristic electrolyte disturbances like hyponatremia and hyperkalemia, which are direct consequences of mineralocorticoid (aldosterone) deficiency. However, these findings are not pathognomonic. The definitive diagnosis requires provocative testing to assess the adrenal gland's functional reserve. The cornerstone is the ACTH stimulation test (Cosyntropin test), which directly challenges the adrenal cortex's ability to produce cortisol. A failed response confirms adrenal insufficiency. Subsequently, measuring a baseline plasma ACTH level is crucial to differentiate primary (adrenal-level) from secondary (pituitary-level) insufficiency. In primary disease, the pituitary's attempt to stimulate the failing adrenal glands leads to markedly elevated ACTH levels, confirming the diagnosis and explaining the classic hyperpigmentation.

initial_lab_findings.item: * **Hyponatremia**: Explanation: Caused by a combination of factors. Aldosterone deficiency leads to urinary sodium wasting. Additionally, chronic cortisol deficiency causes a non-osmotic, persistent release of ADH from the posterior pituitary, leading to free water retention and dilutional hyponatremia.

* **Hyperkalemia**: Explanation: This is a hallmark of mineralocorticoid deficiency. Aldosterone normally promotes potassium excretion in the distal renal tubules. Its absence leads to impaired potassium secretion and subsequent retention, causing hyperkalemia.

* **Non-Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis**: Explanation: Aldosterone also facilitates the secretion of hydrogen ions (H+) in the renal collecting ducts. Without aldosterone, this process is impaired, leading to a mild H+ retention and a subsequent hyperchloremic, non-anion gap metabolic acidosis.

* **Hypoglycemia**: Explanation: Cortisol is a crucial glucocorticoid that promotes gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis, acting as a counter-regulatory hormone to insulin. Cortisol deficiency impairs the body's ability to maintain glucose levels, particularly during periods of fasting or stress.

* **Eosinophilia, Lymphocytosis, Neutropenia**: Explanation: Cortisol normally suppresses the number of circulating eosinophils and lymphocytes and increases neutrophils. Its absence leads to a relative increase in eosinophils and lymphocytes and a decrease in neutrophils.

* **Elevated BUN and Creatinine (Prerenal Azotemia)**: Explanation: Hypovolemia resulting from urinary sodium and water loss (due to aldosterone deficiency) leads to decreased renal perfusion, causing a pre-renal acute kidney injury.

confirmatory_testing.item: * **8 AM Serum Cortisol and Plasma ACTH**: Explanation: A simultaneously drawn morning sample is the best initial screening test. In primary adrenal insufficiency, the classic finding is a low serum cortisol (<5 mcg/dL) despite a markedly elevated plasma ACTH level (>200 pg/mL). This result reflects the pituitary's futile attempt to stimulate a non-responsive adrenal gland, demonstrating a breakdown in the negative feedback loop.

* **ACTH Stimulation Test (Cosyntropin Test)**: Explanation: This is the gold standard for diagnosis. It involves administering an IV or IM dose of synthetic ACTH (cosyntropin) and measuring serum cortisol at baseline, 30, and 60 minutes. An inadequate cortisol response (e.g., a peak cortisol <18-20 mcg/dL) confirms adrenal insufficiency. The gland is unable to 'ramp up' production when stimulated.

* **Plasma Renin Activity (PRA) and Aldosterone**: Explanation: These tests assess the mineralocorticoid axis. In primary adrenal insufficiency, the destruction of the adrenal cortex leads to low aldosterone levels. The resulting volume depletion and hyperkalemia stimulate the renin-angiotensin system, causing a significantly elevated plasma renin activity. This combination of high renin and low aldosterone is specific for primary disease.

* **21-Hydroxylase Antibodies (Anti-21-Hydroxylase Ab)**: Explanation: In developed countries, autoimmune destruction is the most common cause of Addison disease. Measuring these antibodies helps confirm an autoimmune etiology. Their presence is highly specific and is found in over 85% of patients with autoimmune primary adrenal insufficiency.

* **DHEA-S (Dehydroepiandrosterone Sulfate)**: Explanation: DHEA-S is an adrenal androgen produced exclusively in the adrenal cortex. Levels will be very low in Addison disease due to the destruction of adrenal tissue. While not a primary diagnostic test, it supports the diagnosis of adrenal failure.

differentiating_primary_vs_secondary_ins.primary: High. The pituitary gland produces excess ACTH in an attempt to stimulate the failing adrenal glands.
differentiating_primary_vs_secondary_ins.secondary: Low or Inappropriately Normal. The primary defect is in the pituitary, which fails to produce sufficient ACTH.

differentiating_primary_vs_secondary_ins.primary: Present. High levels of ACTH are derived from the precursor molecule pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC). POMC is also cleaved into melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH). Excess POMC production leads to excess MSH, causing hyperpigmentation, especially in sun-exposed areas, palmar creases, and mucous membranes.
differentiating_primary_vs_secondary_ins.secondary: Absent. ACTH and MSH levels are low, so there is no stimulus for increased melanin production. Patients may appear pale.

differentiating_primary_vs_secondary_ins.primary: Impaired. Aldosterone production is deficient because the adrenal gland is destroyed. This leads to high plasma renin activity, hyperkalemia, and orthostatic hypotension.
differentiating_primary_vs_secondary_ins.secondary: Intact. The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) is primarily regulated by renal perfusion and potassium levels, not ACTH. Therefore, aldosterone production is preserved, and hyperkalemia is not a feature.

differentiating_primary_vs_secondary_ins.primary: Flat Response. The adrenal glands are destroyed or atrophied and cannot respond to exogenous ACTH stimulation.
differentiating_primary_vs_secondary_ins.secondary: Suboptimal but present response (initially). With prolonged adrenal atrophy from lack of stimulation, the response becomes blunted over time. A prolonged ACTH stimulation test (over several days) may show a stepwise increase in cortisol, but this is rarely performed clinically.

imaging.purpose: Once the biochemical diagnosis of primary adrenal insufficiency is confirmed, an adrenal CT is performed to determine the underlying etiology. Findings can include small, atrophic glands (suggesting autoimmune adrenalitis), bilateral enlargement or calcification (suggesting infection like TB or fungal disease, or infiltration), or evidence of bilateral adrenal hemorrhage.

riskFactors: Personal or family history of other autoimmune disorders (e.g., Hashimoto's thyroiditis, type 1 diabetes, vitiligo, pernicious anemia)
Polyglandular Autoimmune Syndrome (APS-1, APS-2)
Infections such as tuberculosis, systemic fungal infections, or HIV/AIDS
Malignancy with potential for adrenal metastases (e.g., lung cancer, breast cancer)
Sepsis, particularly with meningococcemia (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome)
Use of anticoagulant medications
Adrenal surgery or trauma
content.epidemiology: *   **Prevalence:** ~100-140 per million in Western countries. *   **Peak Incidence:** 30-50 years of age. *   **Sex:** Autoimmune Addison's is more common in women (2-3:1).
examFindings: **Hyperpigmentation:** Diffuse hyperpigmentation of sun-exposed areas, pressure points (knuckles, elbows), palmar creases, and recent scars. Pathognomonic finding is hyperpigmentation of the buccal mucosa and gums.
**Orthostatic Hypotension:** A drop in systolic blood pressure of 20 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure of 10 mmHg within three minutes of standing.
**Hypotension:** Low resting blood pressure.
**Signs of Dehydration:** Tachycardia, dry mucous membranes, decreased skin turgor.
**Cachexia:** Evidence of weight loss and muscle wasting in chronic disease.
**Vitiligo:** May be present in cases of autoimmune etiology.
**Scant axillary and pubic hair** in female patients.
**Salt craving**: Due to mineralocorticoid deficiency
complications: **Adrenal (Addisonian) Crisis:** A life-threatening state of circulatory collapse with severe hypotension, shock, and altered mental status, typically triggered by physiologic stress (infection, trauma, surgery) in a patient with undiagnosed or undertreated adrenal insufficiency.
**Iatrogenic Cushing's Syndrome:** Can result from chronic glucocorticoid over-replacement, leading to osteoporosis, glucose intolerance, hypertension, and immunosuppression.
**Associated Autoimmune Conditions:** High prevalence of other autoimmune diseases, including Hashimoto's thyroiditis, Type 1 Diabetes, and pernicious anemia.
**Premature Ovarian Insufficiency:** Common in women with autoimmune adrenalitis.
**Increased Cardiovascular and All-Cause Mortality:** Patients have a higher mortality rate compared to the general population, often due to acute adrenal crisis or cardiovascular events.

content.clinicalPresentation: The onset is typically insidious and non-specific, often delaying diagnosis. Symptoms worsen during periods of stress (infection, surgery, trauma). The classic presentation is a patient with chronic fatigue, weakness, and weight loss who develops hypotension and shock during an acute illness (**Adrenal Crisis**).
content.etiologyPathophysiology: Primary adrenal insufficiency results from the progressive destruction of all three layers of the adrenal cortex, leading to a deficiency of glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids, and adrenal androgens. The most common cause in developed countries is autoimmune adrenalitis (over 80% of cases), often associated with Polyglandular Autoimmune Syndrome Type 1 or 2. Globally, infectious causes, particularly tuberculosis, are more prevalent. Other causes include metastatic cancer (lung, breast, melanoma), adrenal hemorrhage (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome in meningococcemia, anticoagulation), infiltration (amyloidosis, sarcoidosis), and certain medications (e.g., ketoconazole, etomidate). The pathophysiology stems from the hormonal deficits: 1) **Cortisol deficiency** impairs gluconeogenesis, leading to hypoglycemia, and causes profound fatigue, weakness, anorexia, and GI disturbances. Loss of negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary results in overproduction of pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC), which is cleaved into ACTH and melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH), causing the characteristic hyperpigmentation. 2) **Aldosterone deficiency** leads to renal salt (Na+) wasting and potassium (K+) retention, resulting in volume depletion, hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and metabolic acidosis. 3) **Adrenal androgen (DHEA) deficiency** primarily affects women, causing loss of libido and sparse axillary/pubic hair.

content.overview: Adrenal crisis, also known as an addisonian crisis or acute adrenal insufficiency, is a life-threatening endocrine emergency characterized by the body's inability to produce an adequate amount of cortisol in response to a physiological stressor. This leads to a state of profound circulatory collapse (shock), severe hypotension, and metabolic derangements. It represents the acute, severe manifestation of adrenal insufficiency, which can be pre-existing (either diagnosed or undiagnosed) or can occur acutely due to adrenal gland destruction. Immediate recognition and treatment are critical to prevent mortality.
symptoms: Profound weakness, fatigue, and lethargy
Nausea, vomiting, and diffuse abdominal pain (can mimic an acute surgical abdomen)
Fever (may be from underlying infection or cortisol deficiency itself)
Dizziness, postural hypotension, and syncope
Confusion, disorientation, psychosis, or coma
Myalgias and arthralgias
Salt craving (in patients with pre-existing primary AI)
content.prognosis: *   With prompt recognition and aggressive treatment, the prognosis is excellent, and patients can recover fully from the acute crisis. *   Delayed diagnosis or treatment is associated with high mortality.
treatment: Immediate administration of IV Hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus, followed by 50-100 mg IV every 6-8 hours or a continuous infusion of 200 mg/24h. Do not delay for diagnostic tests.
Aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation with Isotonic Saline (0.9% NaCl); use Dextrose 5% in Normal Saline (D5NS) if the patient is hypoglycemic.
Correction of severe hypoglycemia with IV dextrose (e.g., 25-50g of D50W if severe).
Identification and aggressive treatment of the underlying precipitating cause (e.g., empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics for suspected infection after obtaining cultures).
Management of severe hyperkalemia, although this often corrects with volume resuscitation and cortisol replacement which has mineralocorticoid activity.
management: Lifelong glucocorticoid replacement (e.g., hydrocortisone, prednisone) with doses split to mimic the normal diurnal rhythm (e.g., two-thirds in the morning, one-third in the late afternoon).
Mineralocorticoid replacement with fludrocortisone for patients with primary adrenal insufficiency to manage salt and water balance.
Strict patient education on 'Sick Day Rules': doubling or tripling the daily glucocorticoid dose during minor illness, fever, or stress.
Provision of an emergency injection kit (e.g., Solu-Cortef) and training for the patient and family on its administration for situations like severe vomiting or trauma.
Wearing a medical alert bracelet or necklace at all times to inform healthcare providers of the condition in an emergency.
Regular follow-up with an endocrinologist to monitor for signs of over- or under-replacement and adjust medication dosages.
riskFactors: Known adrenal insufficiency (primary, secondary, or tertiary)
Chronic glucocorticoid therapy (especially with abrupt cessation or failure to increase dose during stress)
Sepsis, particularly meningococcemia (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome)
Bilateral adrenal hemorrhage or infarction (e.g., due to anticoagulation, trauma, or coagulopathy)
Pituitary apoplexy
Autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes
Major trauma, surgery, or critical illness in a patient with un-diagnosed adrenal insufficiency
content.epidemiology: *   Relatively rare but carries significant mortality if not treated promptly. *   Incidence in patients with known primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease) is approximately 6-8 episodes per 100 patient-years. *   Mortality rate for an adrenal crisis episode is approximately 5-10%, even with modern treatment.
examFindings: Severe hypotension, often refractory to IV fluids and vasopressors
Tachycardia and significant orthostatic hypotension
Signs of hypovolemia and dehydration (e.g., dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor)
Altered mental status, ranging from confusion to obtundation or coma
Hyperpigmentation of skin (especially in sun-exposed areas, palmar creases, knuckles) and mucous membranes (buccal mucosa) is a classic finding of chronic primary adrenal insufficiency
Diffuse abdominal tenderness without localized findings
complications: Refractory circulatory shock leading to multi-organ failure
Severe hypoglycemia resulting in seizures and permanent neurologic damage
Life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias secondary to severe hyperkalemia
Coma
Death if not recognized and treated emergently

content.clinicalPresentation: The classic presentation is a patient with known (or undiagnosed) adrenal insufficiency who develops an acute illness (e.g., gastroenteritis, pneumonia) and presents with **shock that is refractory to IV fluids and vasopressors**. The patient appears critically ill, often with altered mental status. The presentation can be nonspecific and mimic other severe conditions like septic shock or an acute abdomen.
content.etiologyPathophysiology: **Pathophysiology:** The crisis is driven by a profound deficiency of two key adrenal hormones: 1.  **Glucocorticoids (Cortisol):** Cortisol is essential for life. Its deficiency leads to: *   **Cardiovascular Collapse:** Decreased vascular tone and reduced sensitivity of blood vessels to catecholamines (like norepinephrine), leading to profound vasodilation and hypotension. *   **Hypoglycemia:** Impaired gluconeogenesis and increased peripheral glucose utilization. *   **Exaggerated Inflammatory Response:** Cortisol normally dampens the inflammatory response; its absence allows for an uncontrolled release of inflammatory cytokines, contributing to fever and shock. 2.  **Mineralocorticoids (Aldosterone):** Deficiency is prominent in primary adrenal insufficiency. Aldosterone is critical for sodium and water retention and potassium excretion. Its deficiency leads to: *   **Hypovolemia:** Renal salt wasting (hyponatremia) and subsequent water loss. *   **Hyperkalemia & Metabolic Acidosis:** Impaired renal excretion of potassium (K+) and hydrogen (H+) ions.  **Etiology (Causes):** Adrenal crisis is typically precipitated by a stressor in a patient with underlying adrenal insufficiency. 1.  **Stress in a Patient with Chronic Adrenal Insufficiency:** This is the most common cause. *   **Primary Adrenal Insufficiency (Addison's Disease):** Autoimmune adrenalitis, TB, metastatic cancer, adrenal hemorrhage. *   **Secondary/Tertiary Adrenal Insufficiency:** Pituitary or hypothalamic disease. *   **Precipitating Stressors:** Infection (most common), trauma, surgery, dehydration, myocardial infarction, emotional stress. 2.  **Sudden Withdrawal of Long-Term Glucocorticoid Therapy:** Chronic steroid use suppresses the HPA axis, causing adrenal atrophy. Abruptly stopping the medication leaves the patient unable to produce endogenous cortisol. 3.  **Acute Adrenal Hemorrhage or Infarction:** *   **Waterhouse-Friderichsen Syndrome:** Bilateral adrenal hemorrhage classically associated with severe sepsis, especially **Neisseria meningitidis** infection. *   Other causes: Anticoagulant therapy, trauma, coagulopathy. 4.  **Pituitary Apoplexy:** Sudden hemorrhage or infarction of a pituitary adenoma, leading to acute secondary adrenal insufficiency.

diagnostics.overview: The diagnosis of adrenal crisis is primarily clinical and must be suspected in any patient presenting with refractory shock, especially with a history of adrenal insufficiency or chronic steroid use. The classic triad of hypotension, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia is highly suggestive but not always present, particularly in secondary adrenal insufficiency where mineralocorticoid function is preserved. The diagnostic process is a race against time; treatment must be initiated immediately based on high clinical suspicion, often before definitive laboratory confirmation is available. The key is recognizing that a 'normal' cortisol level in a critically ill patient is profoundly abnormal, as a robust stress response should elevate cortisol significantly. Initial laboratory evaluation aims to identify the characteristic metabolic derangements (electrolyte shifts, hypoglycemia, acidosis) that support the diagnosis. Blood for cortisol and ACTH levels should be drawn *before* administering glucocorticoids if possible, but this must not delay life-saving treatment. Confirmatory testing, such as the ACTH stimulation test, is performed after the patient is stabilized to formally establish the diagnosis of adrenal insufficiency and determine its etiology (primary vs. secondary).

labFindings.explanation: Mechanism: A hallmark finding resulting from two primary mechanisms. 1) Aldosterone deficiency (in primary AI) leads to profound renal sodium wasting. 2) Cortisol deficiency and hypovolemia both serve as potent non-osmotic stimuli for ADH (vasopressin) release, leading to free water retention and dilutional hyponatremia. This is a critical electrolyte abnormality to recognize.

Mechanism: Primarily seen in primary adrenal insufficiency due to aldosterone deficiency. Aldosterone normally promotes potassium excretion in the distal nephron via ROMK and BK channels. Its absence leads to impaired potassium secretion and subsequent severe, life-threatening hyperkalemia, which can manifest with characteristic EKG changes.

Mechanism: Cortisol is a crucial counter-regulatory hormone that opposes insulin. Its functions include stimulating hepatic gluconeogenesis and inhibiting glucose uptake in peripheral tissues. In a state of cortisol deficiency, these processes are impaired, leading to an increased risk of hypoglycemia, particularly during periods of stress or poor oral intake.

Mechanism: This results from a combination of factors. Hypovolemia and shock can cause a lactic acidosis (anion gap). More specifically to primary AI, aldosterone deficiency impairs the normal secretion of hydrogen ions (H+) in the renal collecting ducts, leading to a type 4 renal tubular acidosis (hyperkalemic, non-anion gap metabolic acidosis).

Mechanism: Severe volume depletion from mineralocorticoid deficiency (sodium and water loss) leads to decreased renal perfusion. This manifests as an elevated BUN and creatinine with a BUN:Cr ratio > 20:1, indicative of a pre-renal acute kidney injury. This resolves with aggressive fluid resuscitation.

Mechanism: Glucocorticoids normally induce apoptosis of eosinophils and lymphocytes and sequester them in lymphoid tissue. In cortisol deficiency, this suppressive effect is lost, potentially leading to relative or absolute increases in eosinophil and lymphocyte counts on a complete blood count (CBC). While non-specific, their presence in a shocked patient can be a clue.

confirmatoryTesting.explanation: How to Use: Draw blood for these levels *immediately* upon suspicion, *before* giving hydrocortisone, but do not delay treatment. A random cortisol < 5 mcg/dL is highly suggestive. A cortisol level > 20 mcg/dL in a critically ill patient effectively rules out adrenal crisis. The pattern differentiates the cause: High ACTH with low cortisol suggests primary AI (gland failure). Low/normal ACTH with low cortisol suggests secondary/tertiary AI (pituitary/hypothalamic failure).

The Gold Standard: This test is the definitive method for diagnosing primary adrenal insufficiency but is performed *after* the patient is stable. Procedure: A baseline cortisol is drawn, then 250 mcg of cosyntropin (synthetic ACTH) is given IV/IM. Cortisol is remeasured at 30 and 60 minutes. An adequate response is a peak cortisol level >18-20 mcg/dL. A blunted response (failure to stimulate) confirms primary adrenal insufficiency.

Differentiating Primary vs. Secondary AI: This panel helps pinpoint the level of the defect. In primary AI, the failing adrenal gland cannot produce aldosterone, leading to low aldosterone levels and a compensatory, markedly elevated plasma renin activity. In secondary/tertiary AI, the HPA axis failure does not significantly affect the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, so both renin and aldosterone are typically low or normal.

Assessing for Complications: An electrocardiogram is crucial, not for diagnosing the crisis itself, but for detecting the life-threatening cardiac effects of hyperkalemia. Look for peaked T waves (early), PR interval prolongation, QRS widening, and eventual sine wave pattern preceding asystole. These findings demand immediate intervention for hyperkalemia.

Identifying Etiology: Performed after stabilization, an adrenal CT scan can help identify the underlying cause of primary adrenal insufficiency. Findings may include small, atrophic glands (autoimmune), adrenal enlargement/hemorrhage (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome), calcifications (tuberculosis, fungal infection), or bilateral metastases.

diagnosticPitfalls.explanation: The most critical error. Adrenal crisis is a medical emergency. Treatment with IV hydrocortisone and fluids should be initiated immediately based on clinical suspicion. A delay of even one hour to wait for lab results can be fatal.

In a septic or hypotensive patient, the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis should be maximally stimulated. A random cortisol level of 15 mcg/dL, while in the normal range for a healthy person at rest, is inappropriately low for a critically ill patient and strongly suggests adrenal insufficiency.

Patients with secondary adrenal insufficiency (e.g., from abrupt cessation of chronic steroids) will NOT have hyperkalemia because mineralocorticoid production is preserved. Their presentation may be dominated by refractory hypotension and hypoglycemia without the classic electrolyte triad, leading to diagnostic confusion with sepsis.

Hydrocortisone is structurally identical to cortisol and will be measured as such in cortisol assays, making post-treatment levels uninterpretable. Dexamethasone does not cross-react. Therefore, if the diagnosis is truly uncertain and a stimulation test is planned, dexamethasone can be used for initial resuscitation without confounding subsequent test results.

The nonspecific presentation of fever, altered mental status, abdominal pain, and shock has a broad differential. It is frequently misdiagnosed as septic shock, an acute abdomen, myocardial infarction, or even diabetic ketoacidosis (due to vomiting and acidosis). The key differentiator is hypotension that is refractory to aggressive fluid and vasopressor administration.

content.overview: Hyperaldosteronism is a condition characterized by the excessive production of aldosterone by the adrenal cortex. It is a leading cause of secondary hypertension. It is broadly divided into two categories: 1.  **Primary Hyperaldosteronism (Conn Syndrome):** Aldosterone release is independent of the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS). This results in a suppressed renin level. 2.  **Secondary Hyperaldosteronism:** Aldosterone release is a result of appropriate RAAS activation due to decreased renal perfusion or other stimuli. This results in an elevated renin level.  The classic triad of findings is **hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis**. However, many patients present with normal potassium levels.
symptoms: Often asymptomatic, identified during hypertension workup.
Symptoms of hypertension: headaches, dizziness, facial flushing.
Symptoms of hypokalemia: muscle weakness, fatigue, cramping, paresthesias, palpitations.
Symptoms of severe hypokalemia/alkalosis: polyuria and polydipsia (due to hypokalemia-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus), tetany (rare).
content.prognosis: *   **Unilateral Disease (Post-Adrenalectomy):** Excellent. Hypokalemia is cured in >99% of cases. Hypertension is cured or significantly improved. The risk of end-organ damage is reduced. *   **Bilateral Disease (Medical Management):** Good with medication adherence. BP can be well-controlled and hypokalemia corrected, reducing long-term cardiovascular risk. Requires lifelong therapy and monitoring.
treatment: **Goals:** Normalize blood pressure, correct hypokalemia, and mitigate long-term cardiovascular damage from aldosterone excess.
**Unilateral Disease (Adenoma or Unilateral Hyperplasia):**
* **Laparoscopic Adrenalectomy:** The definitive treatment. Cures hypokalemia in >99% and hypertension in ~30-60% of cases, with improvement in BP control for most others.
* Preoperative management includes blood pressure control and potassium correction with a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (MRA).
**Bilateral Adrenal Hyperplasia (BAH/IHA):**
* **Medical Management:** This is the treatment of choice as surgery is not effective.
* **First-line:** Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists (MRAs).
* **Spironolactone:** A non-selective MRA; potent but can cause gynecomastia, erectile dysfunction, and menstrual irregularities.
* **Eplerenone:** A selective MRA with fewer anti-androgenic side effects but is less potent and often requires twice-daily dosing.
* **Adjunctive Therapy:** Potassium-sparing diuretics (e.g., Amiloride) that block ENaC can be added if MRAs are not tolerated or are insufficient.
**Glucocorticoid-Remediable Aldosteronism (GRA):**
* Low-dose physiologic glucocorticoids (e.g., dexamethasone, prednisone) to suppress ACTH-driven aldosterone production.
management: **Dietary Modification:** All patients should be advised to follow a low-sodium diet (<100 mmol or <2.3g/day) to enhance the efficacy of medical therapy and improve blood pressure control.

**Pharmacologic Monitoring (for medically managed patients):** Regular monitoring of serum potassium and creatinine is essential, especially upon initiation and titration of MRA therapy, to screen for hyperkalemia and renal impairment.
**Post-Surgical Monitoring (post-adrenalectomy):**
* Monitor blood pressure and electrolytes. Many patients still require some antihypertensive medication post-operatively.
* Watch for transient hypoaldosteronism and hyperkalemia due to suppression of the contralateral adrenal gland, which may require temporary fludrocortisone replacement.
riskFactors: Resistant hypertension (uncontrolled on 3 antihypertensive agents)
Hypertension with spontaneous or diuretic-induced hypokalemia
Hypertension with an adrenal incidentaloma
Hypertension with obstructive sleep apnea
Hypertension with a family history of primary hyperaldosteronism or early-onset stroke (<40 years)
All first-degree relatives of patients with confirmed primary hyperaldosteronism
content.epidemiology: *   The most common cause of secondary hypertension. *   Affects 5-10% of all patients with hypertension and up to 20% of patients with resistant hypertension. *   Peak incidence is between 30-60 years of age. *   **Aldosterone-producing adenomas** are slightly more common in women. *   **Bilateral hyperplasia** has an equal sex distribution.
examFindings: Hypertension: The primary and often sole physical finding; may be moderate, severe, or drug-resistant.
Absence of peripheral edema, due to the 'aldosterone escape' phenomenon (pressure natriuresis).
Signs of hypokalemia may be present, though often absent: muscle weakness (myopathy), decreased deep tendon reflexes (hyporeflexia).
Positive Chvostek or Trousseau signs (rare, only with severe metabolic alkalosis).
complications: High aldosterone levels have direct, BP-independent toxic effects on end organs.

**Cardiovascular:** Increased risk of myocardial fibrosis, left ventricular hypertrophy, diastolic dysfunction, atrial fibrillation, stroke, and myocardial infarction compared to patients with essential hypertension at similar blood pressures.
**Renal:** Glomerular hyperfiltration, albuminuria, and accelerated progression of chronic kidney disease. Chronic hypokalemia can lead to nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and interstitial nephritis.
**Metabolic:** Impaired insulin sensitivity and secretion, leading to an increased risk of developing glucose intolerance and type 2 diabetes mellitus.
content.clinicalPresentation: A typical patient is a 30- to 60-year-old with difficult-to-control hypertension. They may have been on multiple antihypertensive medications for years with poor response. They may present with symptoms related to hypokalemia, such as muscle weakness or cramping, or be entirely asymptomatic aside from the elevated blood pressure found on routine examination.
content.etiologyPathophysiology:
Primary hyperaldosteronism results from autonomous aldosterone secretion from the adrenal cortex, independent of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS). The most common causes are: 1. **Bilateral Adrenal Hyperplasia (BAH)**, also known as Idiopathic Hyperaldosteronism (IHA), accounting for ~60% of cases. 2. **Aldosterone-Producing Adenoma (APA)**, the classic 'Conn Syndrome', accounting for ~35% of cases. Rarer causes include unilateral adrenal hyperplasia, familial hyperaldosteronism (e.g., glucocorticoid-remediable aldosteronism), and adrenocortical carcinoma. 

**Pathophysiology:** The excessive, unregulated aldosterone binds to mineralocorticoid receptors in the principal cells of the renal distal convoluted tubules and collecting ducts. This upregulates the activity of the apical epithelial sodium channel (ENaC), leading to increased sodium and water reabsorption, which causes volume expansion and hypertension. It also increases the secretion of potassium via the renal outer medullary potassium (ROMK) channel and hydrogen ions via H+-ATPase, resulting in hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis, respectively. The resulting volume expansion and hypertension suppress renin release from the juxtaglomerular apparatus, creating the hallmark biochemical profile of high aldosterone and low renin.

hyperaldosteronism_conn_syndrome.overview: Primary hyperaldosteronism (PA), also known as Conn syndrome when caused by an adenoma, is a disorder characterized by the autonomous, renin-independent overproduction of aldosterone from the adrenal cortex. This represents the most common cause of secondary hypertension, affecting 5-10% of all hypertensive patients. The primary etiologies are a unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma (APA) or bilateral adrenal hyperplasia (BAH). The pathophysiologic cornerstone is aldosterone excess acting on mineralocorticoid receptors in the distal nephron. This upregulates the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) and the Na+/K+-ATPase pump, leading to avid sodium and water reabsorption, which expands extracellular volume and causes hypertension. Concurrently, it promotes potassium and hydrogen ion excretion, leading to potential hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis. Importantly, renin secretion from the juxtaglomerular apparatus is suppressed due to negative feedback from the volume expansion and high blood pressure. Beyond its renal effects, aldosterone exerts direct, blood pressure-independent damaging effects on the cardiovascular system, promoting myocardial fibrosis, vascular inflammation, and endothelial dysfunction, leading to a higher risk of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality compared to patients with essential hypertension at the same blood pressure level.

symptoms.name: Resistant Hypertension
symptoms.description:
* **Concept**: The cardinal clinical feature. It is often severe, difficult to control, and requires multiple antihypertensive agents. 
* **Mechanism**: Continuous, unregulated aldosterone-mediated sodium and water retention leads to chronic volume expansion. This mechanism is non-responsive to conventional renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) inhibitors (like ACEi/ARBs) because the system's starting point (renin) is already suppressed.

symptoms.name: Muscle Weakness and Cramping
symptoms.description:
* **Concept**: Often described as profound fatigue or inability to perform physical tasks. 
* **Mechanism**: Result of hypokalemia. Low extracellular potassium hyperpolarizes the resting membrane potential of skeletal muscle cells, making them less excitable and impairing their ability to contract properly.

symptoms.name: Paresthesias and Tetany
symptoms.description:
* **Concept**: Sensations of numbness, tingling, or spontaneous muscle spasms.
* **Mechanism**: Caused by severe hypokalemia and concomitant metabolic alkalosis. The alkalosis reduces the level of ionized calcium in the blood (by increasing its binding to albumin), which lowers the threshold for neuronal depolarization and leads to increased neuromuscular excitability.

symptoms.name: Headaches
symptoms.description:
* **Concept**: Frequent and often severe headaches, typically related to the degree of hypertension. 
* **Mechanism**: Directly attributable to the elevated intracranial pressure and vascular strain from severe, sustained hypertension.

symptoms.name: Polyuria and Polydipsia
symptoms.description:
* **Concept**: Increased frequency of urination and excessive thirst. 
* **Mechanism**: Chronic hypokalemia impairs the kidney's ability to concentrate urine by inducing resistance to antidiuretic hormone (ADH) in the collecting ducts, a condition known as nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. The resulting water loss (polyuria) triggers a compensatory thirst mechanism (polydipsia).

symptoms.name: Asymptomatic
symptoms.description:
* **Concept**: Many patients, especially those with normal potassium levels, may only have hypertension and no other complaints.
* **Mechanism**: The classic triad of hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis is present in a minority of patients. Normokalemic hypertension is the most common presentation, making screening in resistant hypertension crucial.

complications.name: Increased Cardiovascular Morbidity/Mortality
complications.description:
* **Concept**: Patients with PA have a higher incidence of stroke, myocardial infarction, and atrial fibrillation than patients with essential hypertension, even when matched for blood pressure levels.
* **Mechanism**: Aldosterone has direct, non-genomic effects on cardiovascular tissue. It promotes myocardial and perivascular fibrosis, inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, and oxidative stress, leading to structural and functional damage independent of its hypertensive effects.

complications.name: Left Ventricular Hypertrophy (LVH)
complications.description:
* **Concept**: Thickening of the heart's left ventricle wall.
* **Mechanism**: A consequence of both the increased afterload from chronic hypertension (pressure overload) and the direct pro-fibrotic effects of aldosterone on cardiac myocytes.

complications.name: Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)
complications.description:
* **Concept**: Progressive decline in renal function over time.
* **Mechanism**: Sustained systemic hypertension causes intraglomerular hypertension and hyperfiltration, leading to glomerulosclerosis. Aldosterone also contributes directly by promoting renal inflammation and fibrosis.

complications.name: Metabolic Syndrome and Type 2 Diabetes
complications.description:
* **Concept**: Increased risk of developing insulin resistance and diabetes.
* **Mechanism**: Hypokalemia directly impairs insulin secretion from pancreatic β-cells. Additionally, aldosterone itself may contribute to insulin resistance in peripheral tissues.

complications.name: Severe Metabolic Alkalosis
complications.description:
* **Concept**: Elevated serum bicarbonate (HCO3-) and blood pH.
* **Mechanism**: In the distal nephron's intercalated cells, aldosterone stimulates the apical H+-ATPase pump, increasing the secretion of hydrogen ions into the urine. This loss of acid from the body results in a systemic metabolic alkalosis.

examFindings.name: Sustained Hypertension
examFindings.description:
* **Concept**: The most consistent physical exam finding is an elevated blood pressure reading. Diastolic hypertension is often prominent.
* **Mechanism**: Chronic volume expansion due to aldosterone-mediated sodium and water retention.

examFindings.name: Absence of Significant Edema
examFindings.description:
* **Concept**: Despite sodium and water retention, peripheral edema is typically not a feature.
* **Mechanism**: This is due to the 'aldosterone escape' phenomenon. After initial volume expansion, pressure natriuresis and increased levels of atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) promote renal sodium excretion, preventing further volume gain and establishing a new, higher-pressure steady state without causing overt edema.

examFindings.name: Signs of Left Ventricular Hypertrophy
examFindings.description:
* **Concept**: On cardiac auscultation or palpation, signs of LVH may be present in long-standing disease.
* **Mechanism**: A sustained, forceful apical impulse (LV heave) or an S4 gallop (sound of atrial contraction into a stiff, non-compliant ventricle) may be detected, reflecting the heart's adaptation to chronic pressure overload.

examFindings.name: Hypertensive Retinopathy
examFindings.description:
* **Concept**: Funduscopic examination may reveal damage to retinal blood vessels.
* **Mechanism**: Chronic severe hypertension leads to characteristic changes such as arteriolar narrowing (copper/silver wiring), arteriovenous (AV) nicking, hemorrhages, and, in severe cases, papilledema.

examFindings.name: Normal Neurologic Exam (unless complicated)
examFindings.description:
* **Concept**: The baseline neurologic exam is usually normal. However, focal deficits could indicate a prior stroke, a known complication.
* **Mechanism**: While symptoms like weakness or paresthesias may be reported due to electrolyte disturbances, objective findings like focal weakness, sensory loss, or reflex changes are absent unless a cerebrovascular event has occurred.

tests.name: Aldosterone-Renin Ratio (ARR)
tests.description:
* **Concept**: The single best screening test for primary hyperaldosteronism, performed in the morning after the patient has been upright for at least 2 hours.
* **Mechanism**: In PA, aldosterone production is autonomous (high), while renin is suppressed by negative feedback from volume expansion (low). This results in a markedly elevated ratio (e.g., ARR > 20-30). A simultaneously elevated plasma aldosterone concentration (PAC > 15 ng/dL) increases specificity.

confirmation.title: Confirmatory Tests
confirmation.description: These tests are performed to confirm that aldosterone secretion is non-suppressible and autonomous after a positive screening test.

tests.name: Intravenous Saline Infusion Test
tests.description:
* **Concept**: Patient receives an infusion of 2 liters of 0.9% saline over 4 hours.
* **Mechanism**: In a normal individual, this acute volume expansion would suppress aldosterone secretion. In PA, aldosterone remains inappropriately elevated. A post-infusion PAC > 10 ng/dL confirms the diagnosis.

tests.name: Oral Sodium Loading Test
tests.description:
* **Concept**: Patient consumes a high-sodium diet (e.g., >200 mmol/day) for 3 days, and a 24-hour urine collection is performed on the third day.
* **Mechanism**: Similar to saline infusion, a high sodium load should suppress aldosterone. A 24-hour urine aldosterone level > 12 mcg/24h confirms autonomous secretion.

tests.name: Fludrocortisone Suppression Test
tests.description:
* **Concept**: Considered a highly reliable but complex test involving administration of fludrocortisone (a potent synthetic mineralocorticoid) and oral sodium chloride.
* **Mechanism**: Administration of an exogenous mineralocorticoid should completely suppress endogenous aldosterone production. Failure to suppress plasma aldosterone below a certain threshold confirms autonomy.

subtype_classification.title: Subtype Classification
subtype_classification.description: Once PA is biochemically confirmed, imaging and sampling are used to differentiate unilateral disease (adenoma, surgical candidate) from bilateral disease (hyperplasia, medical management).

tests.name: High-Resolution Adrenal CT
tests.description:
* **Concept**: The initial imaging modality to visualize the adrenal glands.
* **Mechanism**: Can identify a unilateral, low-density macroadenoma (>1 cm) or suggest bilateral hyperplasia (diffusely thickened or nodular glands). However, its utility is limited by non-functioning incidentalomas, which increase with age, and the inability to visualize microadenomas.

tests.name: Adrenal Vein Sampling (AVS)
tests.description:
* **Concept**: The gold standard for differentiating unilateral from bilateral aldosterone secretion.
* **Mechanism**: An interventional radiologist cannulates both adrenal veins and the inferior vena cava to measure aldosterone and cortisol levels. A high ratio of aldosterone to cortisol from one adrenal vein compared to the other (lateralization index) definitively identifies a unilateral source, directing the patient to potentially curative surgery (adrenalectomy).

content.overview:
Pheochromocytoma is a rare neuroendocrine tumor arising from the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla that secretes catecholamines (epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine). Tumors arising from extra-adrenal sympathetic ganglia are termed paragangliomas, which are functionally and pathologically similar. Together, they are often referred to as pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma (PPGL). The unregulated and often episodic release of catecholamines leads to the classic clinical presentation of paroxysmal hypertension, headaches, palpitations, and diaphoresis. While most pheochromocytomas are benign, approximately 10-15% can be malignant and metastasize.

The clinical significance of pheochromocytoma lies in its potential to cause life-threatening cardiovascular complications, including hypertensive crisis, myocardial infarction, stroke, aortic dissection, and catecholamine-induced cardiomyopathy. The symptoms can mimic anxiety or panic disorders, leading to delayed diagnosis. Historically, the condition was described by the 'rule of 10s' (10% bilateral, 10% extra-adrenal, 10% malignant, 10% in children), though modern data indicates a much higher rate of genetic inheritance (up to 40%) and malignancy. Prompt diagnosis and appropriate management, which involves careful preoperative alpha- and subsequent beta-adrenergic blockade followed by surgical resection, are critical to prevent morbidity and mortality.
symptoms: Headache (severe, episodic)
Palpitations (forceful or rapid heartbeat)
Diaphoresis (profuse sweating)
Hypertension (paroxysmal or sustained)
Anxiety or panic attacks
Sense of impending doom
Pallor
Tremor
Nausea and vomiting
Abdominal or chest pain
Fatigue and weakness
Unexplained weight loss
Heat intolerance
Constipation
content.prognosis: The prognosis for patients with pheochromocytoma depends largely on whether the tumor is benign or malignant, its complete surgical resection, and the presence of an underlying genetic mutation. For benign, completely resected pheochromocytomas, the prognosis is excellent, with a 5-year survival rate exceeding 95%. However, recurrence can still occur years later, emphasizing the need for lifelong follow-up. For malignant (metastatic) pheochromocytoma, the prognosis is significantly worse and the disease is generally considered incurable. The 5-year survival rate for metastatic disease is highly variable but averages around 50-60%. Prognosis is particularly poor for patients with SDHB mutations, which are associated with a higher risk of malignancy and more aggressive disease. Early detection and complete surgical removal provide the best chance for a cure.
treatment: The definitive treatment for pheochromocytoma is surgical resection. However, meticulous perioperative medical management is essential to prevent a life-threatening hypertensive crisis during surgery.
**Preoperative Medical Management (7-14 days prior to surgery):**
1. **Alpha-Adrenergic Blockade:** This is the FIRST and most critical step. It controls hypertension and allows for volume re-expansion.

*   **Phenoxybenzamine:** An irreversible, non-selective alpha-blocker. Started at a low dose and titrated up until blood pressure is controlled (<130/80 mmHg seated) and mild orthostatic hypotension is achieved.

*   **Selective alpha-1 blockers (Doxazosin, Prazosin, Terazosin):** Reversible blockers that may have fewer side effects (e.g., less reflex tachycardia, shorter duration of postoperative hypotension).

2. **Beta-Adrenergic Blockade:** This is added **ONLY AFTER** adequate alpha-blockade has been established (typically 2-3 days later). It is used to control reflex tachycardia caused by alpha-blockade.
*   Common agents include propranolol or metoprolol.

*   **WARNING:** Initiating beta-blockade before alpha-blockade can lead to unopposed alpha-1 receptor stimulation, causing severe vasoconstriction and a paradoxical, life-threatening hypertensive crisis.

3. **Volume Expansion:** Patients should be encouraged to maintain a high-sodium diet and liberal fluid intake to reverse catecholamine-induced volume contraction. This helps prevent severe hypotension after tumor removal.
**Surgical Management:**
*   **Laparoscopic Adrenalectomy:** The standard of care for most pheochromocytomas. Minimally invasive with faster recovery.
*   **Open Adrenalectomy:** Reserved for very large (>6 cm) or invasive tumors.
*   Requires an experienced surgeon and anesthesia team skilled in managing potential massive intraoperative hemodynamic fluctuations.
**Management of Hypertensive Crisis (Acute):**
*   IV Phentolamine (a reversible alpha-blocker), Sodium Nitroprusside, or Nicardipine.
management: **Postoperative Management:**
*   Patients require monitoring in an ICU or step-down unit immediately post-op.
*   **Hypotension:** Common due to abrupt withdrawal of catecholamines in the setting of residual alpha-blockade and expanded intravascular volume. Often requires vasopressor support initially.
*   **Hypoglycemia:** Catecholamine excess suppresses insulin secretion. After tumor removal, insulin levels can rebound, causing hypoglycemia. Blood glucose should be monitored closely.
*   **Adrenal Insufficiency:** Patients undergoing bilateral adrenalectomy will require lifelong glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement therapy.
**Long-Term Follow-Up:**
*   Lifelong annual biochemical surveillance (plasma or urine metanephrines) is mandatory for all patients, regardless of whether the tumor was benign or malignant.
*   Follow-up is necessary to detect local recurrence, new tumors (especially in genetic cases), or distant metastases.
*   Patients with known genetic mutations may require additional surveillance for other associated tumors (e.g., medullary thyroid cancer in MEN2, renal cell carcinoma in VHL).
**Management of Malignant/Metastatic Disease:**
*   Treatment is palliative, not curative, aimed at controlling symptoms and tumor growth.

*   Options include surgical debulking, systemic chemotherapy (CVD protocol: Cyclophosphamide, Vincristine, Dacarbazine), targeted therapies (e.g., Sunitinib), and radionuclide therapy with high-dose 131I-MIBG or Peptide Receptor Radionuclide Therapy (PRRT) with 177Lu-DOTATATE.
riskFactors: Family history of pheochromocytoma or paraganglioma
Known carrier of a genetic mutation associated with PPGL syndromes

Personal history of an associated genetic syndrome: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 2 (MEN2), Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease, Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), or hereditary paraganglioma syndromes (SDHx mutations)
content.epidemiology: Pheochromocytoma is a rare condition with an estimated annual incidence of 0.8 per 100,000 person-years. It is found in approximately 0.2-0.6% of patients with sustained hypertension. The peak incidence occurs between the ages of 40 and 50, though hereditary forms can present earlier. There is no significant predilection for either sex. While the classic 'Rule of 10s' is often cited for historical context (10% extra-adrenal, 10% bilateral, 10% malignant, 10% in children, 10% familial), modern genetic research and clinical data have shown these proportions to be inaccurate. For instance, the rate of hereditary disease is now estimated to be as high as 40%, the malignancy rate is closer to 15-20% for pheochromocytoma and higher for some paragangliomas (especially SDHB-related), and bilateral tumors are almost exclusively seen in hereditary syndromes.

Tachycardia or other tachyarrhythmias
Orthostatic hypotension
Pallor of the skin
Diaphoresis
Tremor
Hyperglycemia
Stigmata of associated genetic syndromes (e.g., caf-au-lait spots, neurofibromas, mucosal neuromas)
Palpable abdominal mass (rare; palpation may provoke a crisis)
complications: Hypertensive crisis leading to hemorrhagic stroke, myocardial infarction, or aortic dissection
Catecholamine-induced cardiomyopathy (can be reversible, includes Takotsubo-like patterns)
Cardiac arrhythmias (e.g., ventricular tachycardia, atrial fibrillation)
Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and pulmonary edema
Sudden death
Metastasis (in malignant cases) to bone, liver, lymph nodes, and lungs
Postoperative hypotension and hypoglycemia
Surgical complications (bleeding, infection)
Recurrence of the tumor
